Package com.bilt.pos.session

Interface ShopperSession

All Superinterfaces:
AutoCloseable
All Known Subinterfaces:
TerminalShopperSession
public interface ShopperSession extends AutoCloseable
One shopper's visit at a lane, with or without a terminal.

A shopper session is the unit the register opens when a customer steps up and ends when they walk away. It owns the basket being rung — basket() — and the member identified for the visit, if any — member() — and carries the lane's identifiers: the register's sale ID, the currency, and the store location. What it does not have is a device or a settlement: everything that needs a Bilt terminal — identification prompts, customer input, the customer display, stored value, settlement, refunds, and voids — lives on TerminalShopperSession. A lane with a terminal uses TerminalShopperSession.builder(); a lane without one, or a register that only wants the basket model and member state, uses the local session that builder() creates.

Basket mutations are pure local compute: each returns the updated snapshot synchronously and never blocks on a device. A session can ring several baskets in sequence — SessionBasket.clear() is the boundary between them.

A session ends once, with end(), and cannot be restarted or reused afterwards; its basket refuses changes from then on. Like every session operation, end() is lazy: it returns a SessionResult that does nothing until execute() (asynchronous, outcome through the registered handlers) or executeSync() (blocking) is invoked. Sessions are AutoCloseable, so try-with-resources ends them even on exception paths — close() is a best-effort end() that logs rather than throws. 


 try (ShopperSession session = ShopperSession.builder()
         .saleId("POS-LANE-3")
         .currency("USD")
         .start()) {
     session.basket().addItem(
             BasketItem.sale("KRK-CNDL-LRG-VAN", "Large Vanilla Candle", 1, new BigDecimal("24.99")));
     ...
 }

Sessions are intended for use from a single register thread.

    • basket

      SessionBasket basket()
      The session's basket: item and tax mutations, batch edits, and snapshots. Mutations are refused after the session has ended; a terminal session also refuses them while money is moving and after the current basket has settled. Call SessionBasket.clear() to begin another basket in the same session. Each mutation returns the updated snapshot without touching any device.

    • context

      SessionContext context()
      The session's context: the CheckoutPhase and free-form attributes a widget may use, plus the lane identifiers. Mutable at any time from any thread; pure local compute that reaches no device. A terminal session moves the phase itself around settlement — see CheckoutPhase. Writes are refused once the session has ended.

    • member

      void member(Member member)
      Attaches the member for this visit, or clears it with null (signed out). Allowed at any time — before scanning, mid-basket, or after a failed settlement — and on both session types.

      A resolved member (Member.id(String)) attaches immediately with no roundtrip. A member pending resolution (Member.idResolver()) attaches as pending and is resolved in the background on the session's operation lane: on a terminal session by looking the identifier up on the terminal (Nexo BalanceInquiry; account id and phone number only — email and custom identifiers cannot be resolved there, report through onBackgroundError, and stay pending), on a local session not at all yet (the member stays pending). Until a pending member resolves, the visit is treated as a guest's: settlement does not send a member id and getMember() is null. A lookup that finds nobody clears the member; a lookup that fails reports through onBackgroundError and leaves the member pending. Whatever member is attached last wins, so a stale lookup never overwrites a member set after it.

      Every change to the member — from this method, a terminal identification, or a completed lookup — is announced through the builder's onMemberChanged handler.

    • member

      Member member()
      The member attached to this visit, resolved or pending resolution, or null when none is. A terminal session's identification prompt attaches the member it finds here too.

    • widget

      <W extends Widget> W widget(Class<W> type)
      The registered widget of the given type — the runtime handle for pausing, resuming or otherwise driving a widget configured with widget(..) on the builder, e.g. session.widget(RetailMedia.class).pause(). Matches by assignability, so a widget interface works as well as a class.

      A missing widget is a programming error — the set of widgets is fixed on the builder, so asking for one that was never registered means the builder and this call disagree — and throws IllegalArgumentException rather than returning null. Two registered widgets of the type are ambiguous and throw too; pick one from widgets() instead.

    • widgets

      List<Widget> widgets()
      Every registered widget, in registration order; empty for a session without widgets.

    • end

      SessionResult<Void> end()
      Ends the session. After it succeeds no session operation is allowed and the basket is frozen; create a new session for the next shopper. A terminal session also tells the terminal to discard the session-scoped data it accumulated, and may refuse to end while money movement is unresolved — see TerminalShopperSession.end().

    • close

      void close()
      Best-effort end() for try-with-resources: a failure to end, or a lifecycle refusal, is logged, not thrown, and an already-ended session is left alone. Registers that need to react to a failed end should call end() directly. It never bypasses the guards that make end() refuse: automatic resource cleanup must not silently abandon financial recovery.

      Blocking, and queued behind any in-flight operation — so with a callback executor configured, never call it from that executor's thread while operations may be in flight: the in-flight operation may need this thread for its handlers before it can finish, and both would wait forever. UI-driven teardown should use end().execute() with an onComplete instead; close() is for try-with-resources and process-exit paths.
